Sterling

/STUR-ling/ — 'stir' + 'ling', like the famous silver · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sterling is of excellent, proven quality.

Decades of sterling service earned the librarian a park bench dedicated in her honor.

Worked Example

In fifteen years as treasurer, Ms. Vega never misplaced a cent, filed every report early, and earned praise from three separate auditors. When the board needed someone to manage the new endowment, every hand pointed to her.

Ms. Vega's record was sterling — excellent and trustworthy in quality, like genuine silver. 'Good' work merely meets the standard; sterling work is so consistently excellent it becomes a mark of proven value.

How Strong Is It? — solid → sterling → peerless

solid vs. sterling

solid vs. sterling: Solid is weaker than sterling — solid work is dependably good, while sterling work is excellent enough to be held up as proof of quality.

peerless vs. sterling

peerless vs. sterling: Peerless is stronger than sterling — sterling means excellent and proven, but peerless means so excellent that nothing else can even compare.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — steorra (ster-)

root — steorra (ster-): star (Old English)

suffix — -ling

suffix — -ling: small one; one having that quality (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Medieval English silver pennies likely bore a small star — a 'little star' coin, or sterling. Because those coins' silver was reliably pure, sterling came to mean 'of proven, excellent quality.'

Use the root in a new word: duckling
